title: Agent-written code outlives human code in open source — the bottleneck is governance, not generation quality
summary: A large-scale survival analysis on arXiv ('Will It Survive?') tracks more than 200,000 code units across 201 open-source projects to ask how long AI-agent-authored code actually persists once merged. Counter to the common assumption that AI output is disposable scaffolding, agent-authored lines are modified less often than human-written ones — a 15.8 percentage-point lower modification rate and a 16% lower hazard of being changed (HR = 0.842, p < 0.001). The nuance: agent code shows slightly higher corrective (bug-fix) churn, while human code shows more adaptive change, and simple text features can flag which code is modification-prone (AUC-ROC 0.671) but cannot predict when changes happen. The authors' conclusion is the leadership takeaway: the constraint on AI-generated code's long-term value is not raw generation quality but the organizational practices that govern its evolution — review depth, ownership, and how teams decide to revisit code. It reframes 'is the AI code good enough?' as 'do we have the maintenance and ownership discipline to steward it?'
whyItMatters: If agent code persists longer than human code, the durable risk is not throwaway output but under-reviewed code quietly accumulating as long-lived dependency — making review depth and ownership the decisive controls.
Framing the bottleneck as organizational evolution practices, not model quality, shifts the leadership lever from 'pick a better model' to 'fix how we steward merged code.'
Slightly elevated corrective churn in agent code suggests latent defects surface later, arguing for stronger post-merge monitoring rather than one-time review at the gate.
recommendedActions: Assign clear human ownership for merged agent-authored code so long-lived AI contributions are not orphaned in the codebase.
Strengthen review depth and post-merge defect tracking specifically for AI-generated changes, given their longer persistence and corrective-churn profile.
Periodically audit long-lived AI-authored modules rather than assuming they will be naturally refactored away.
risksAndCaveats: Evidence is from public open-source repositories and a preprint (not yet peer-reviewed); enterprise monorepos with different review and ownership norms may behave differently.
Lower modification rate is not by itself a quality verdict — code can persist because it is correct, or because no one is maintaining it; the study cannot fully separate the two.
Data reflects a January 2026 snapshot of agent behavior and tooling, which continues to evolve.
